## Answer

Apply Gram–Schmidt to the columns of $A$. One obtains

$$Q_1=\begin{pmatrix}1/\sqrt2&0&1/\sqrt2\\1/\sqrt2&0&-1/\sqrt2\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad R=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt2&\sqrt2&1/\sqrt2\\0&1&1\\0&0&1/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},$$

so $Q_1^TQ_1=I$, the diagonal of $R$ is positive, and $A=Q_1R$.

For the second factorization, apply Gram–Schmidt to the columns of $A^T$ and transpose the resulting QR decomposition. This gives

$$P=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt3&0&0\\2/\sqrt3&\sqrt6/3&0\\2/\sqrt3&-1/\sqrt6&1/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},$$

$$Q_2=\begin{pmatrix}1/\sqrt3&1/\sqrt3&1/\sqrt3\\1/\sqrt6&1/\sqrt6&-2/\sqrt6\\-1/\sqrt2&1/\sqrt2&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Here $Q_2Q_2^T=I$, $P$ is lower triangular with positive diagonal, and direct multiplication verifies $A=PQ_2$.

## Answer

Orthogonality of $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ gives

$$k=\frac{\alpha_2^T\beta_1}{\beta_1^T\beta_1}=1,$$

so $\beta_1=(1,0,1)^T$ and $\beta_2=(0,2,0)^T$. The last Gram–Schmidt coefficients are therefore

$$l_1=\frac{\alpha_3^T\beta_1}{\beta_1^T\beta_1}=\frac52,\qquad l_2=\frac{\alpha_3^T\beta_2}{\beta_2^T\beta_2}=\frac12.$$

Thus the answer is $\boxed{(A)}$.

## Answer

Every eigenvalue of a real orthogonal matrix has modulus one, and its nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs whose products are $1$. The remaining real eigenvalues are $\pm1$. Since $\det A<0$, an odd number of the real eigenvalues must be $-1$.

Hence $A$ must have the eigenvalue

$$\boxed{-1}.$$

## Answer

Suppose $c_1\alpha_1+c_2\alpha_2+c_3\alpha_3=0$. Applying $A^2$ gives $c_1\alpha_3=0$, hence $c_1=0$. Applying $A$ to the remaining relation gives $c_2\alpha_3=0$, hence $c_2=0$, and then $c_3=0$. Thus $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3$ are linearly independent and form a basis.

In this basis,

$$[A]_{(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Therefore the only eigenvalue is $0$ (algebraic multiplicity three). Since $A(c_1\alpha_1+c_2\alpha_2+c_3\alpha_3)=c_1\alpha_2+c_2\alpha_3$, its eigenspace is

$$E_0=\ker A=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_3\}.$$

Finally, all eigenvalues of $A+2I$ equal $2$, so

$$\det(A+2I)=2^3=\boxed{8}.$$

## Answer

A real symmetric $2\times2$ matrix with the repeated eigenvalue $\lambda$ and two orthogonal eigenvectors is $A=\lambda I$. Moreover, $\alpha_1\alpha_1^T$ has eigenvalue $\|\alpha_1\|^2=k_1$ along $\alpha_1$ and eigenvalue $0$ on its orthogonal complement. Hence

$$A+\alpha_1\alpha_1^T\sim\operatorname{diag}(\lambda+k_1,\lambda).$$

Thus the answer is $\boxed{(B)}$.

## Answer

From $Ax=\mu x$ with $x=(1,b,1)^T$,

$$3+b=\mu,\qquad 2+2b=\mu b,\qquad a+b+1=\mu.$$

The first and third equations give $a=2$; the middle equation then gives $(b-1)(b+2)=0$. In either case the matrix is

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix},$$

whose eigenvalues are $4,1,1$. Consequently

$$\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=4^2+1^2+1^2=18.$$

Thus the answer is $\boxed{(C)}$.

## Answer

Because $A$ is invertible, $AA^*=|A|I$. Multiplying $A^*\alpha=\lambda\alpha$ by $A$ yields

$$A\alpha=\frac{|A|}{\lambda}\alpha.$$

Substituting $\alpha=(1,b,1)^T$ into this eigenvector equation gives $a=2$ and $(b-1)(b+2)=0$. At $a=2$, $|A|=4$. If $b=1$, the corresponding eigenvalue of $A$ is $4$, so $|A|/\lambda=4$ and $\lambda=1$; if $b=-2$, then $\lambda=4$.

Therefore the stated implication that is certainly correct is

$$b=1\Longrightarrow\lambda=1,$$

so the answer is $\boxed{(C)}$.

## Answer

From $A^2=0$, every eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda^2=0$, hence the only eigenvalue is $0$. Also $\operatorname{im}A\subseteq\ker A$, so

$$\operatorname{rank}A\leq\dim\ker A=3-\operatorname{rank}A,$$

which gives $\operatorname{rank}A\leq1$. Since $A\ne0$, $\operatorname{rank}A=1$ and therefore $\dim\ker A=2$. All eigenvectors belong to $\ker A$, so the maximum number of linearly independent eigenvectors is

$$\boxed{2}.$$

Thus the answer is $\boxed{(C)}$.
